metadata.title: ADVISOR: Autonomous Surface Ship for Guidance
metadata.description: EU ITEA Program — Escort-type Autonomous Surface Vehicle for cooperative navigation in constrained maritime environments.

AdvisorPage.title: ADVISOR: Autonomous Surface Ship for Guidance
AdvisorPage.subtitle: EU ITEA Program — Escort-type Autonomous Surface Vehicle
AdvisorPage.overviewText: ADVISOR is an escort-type Autonomous Surface Vehicle (ASV) developed under the EU ITEA program, focusing on autonomous guidance and cooperative navigation in constrained maritime environments including harbors and near-shore areas. The project emphasizes supervised autonomy — where human oversight coexists with automated decision-making — to enable safe, reliable operation in dynamic and cluttered waterways. Field validation is a central component of the program.
AdvisorPage.fieldTrialText: Field trials are conducted in representative maritime environments to validate navigation algorithms, sensor fusion performance, and autonomous decision-making under real operational conditions. The ASV undergoes structured test scenarios including convoy operations, obstacle avoidance, and return-to-base maneuvers.
AdvisorPage.fieldTrialCaption: ADVISOR field trial — autonomous surface vessel in harbor environment
AdvisorPage.fieldTrialImageAlt: Autonomous surface vehicle — Maritime Robotics platform for harbor and escort trials
AdvisorPage.navText: The ADVISOR platform integrates a comprehensive multi-modal sensor suite to achieve robust situational awareness in complex, dynamic maritime environments. Sensor data is fused in real time to support obstacle detection, path planning, and adaptive navigation.
AdvisorPage.bathyText1: In addition to navigation, ADVISOR collects environmental and oceanographic data during operations. Onboard meteorological sensors continuously monitor wind speed, wind direction, air temperature, and atmospheric pressure — providing contextual data that informs route planning and maneuverability analysis.
AdvisorPage.bathyText2: Bathymetric mapping capabilities support harbor surveying and shallow-water navigation, contributing to a richer environmental model that enhances the ASV's autonomous decision-making.
AdvisorPage.bathyCaption: Bathymetry and environmental data collection during field operations
AdvisorPage.bathyImageAlt: 3D bathymetric map on a display: color-coded seafloor depths with survey overlays during operations

metadata.title: Multi-Static Radar Systems
metadata.description: Spatially distributed radar for multi-target tracking and spatial diversity — IEEE RadarConf25 research by D7 Technology.

MultistaticPage.title: Multi-Static Radar Systems
MultistaticPage.subtitle: Spatially distributed radar for multi-target tracking and spatial diversity
MultistaticPage.overviewText: Multi-static radar uses separated transmitters and receivers to observe targets from multiple aspect angles, improving detection robustness for low-RCS (Radar Cross Section) targets and reducing sensitivity to clutter, interference, and stealth shaping. By exploiting spatial diversity, multi-static configurations overcome fundamental limitations of monostatic radar and provide richer measurement geometry for target tracking and classification.
MultistaticPage.simulationText: Simulation environments model the geometric distribution of radar nodes, target trajectories, and measurement uncertainty. Monte Carlo trials across diverse target scenarios are used to validate plot fusion algorithms and assess tracking performance metrics including detection probability, false alarm rate, and positional accuracy.
MultistaticPage.simulationCaption: Multi-static radar simulation map — node distribution and target tracking scenario
MultistaticPage.simulationImageAlt: Multi-panel simulation maps: atmospheric and polarimetric radar fields over west-east and south-north distance in kilometers
MultistaticPage.demoText: The following demonstration illustrates the multi-static radar system processing pipeline, including plot-level data fusion, track initiation, and multi-target tracking performance in a simulated scenario.

metadata.title: Wearable Sensors & Performance Analysis
metadata.description: UWB and IMU-based human motion tracking and performance analysis research by D7 Technology. IEEE SIU 2025 publication.

WearableSensorsPage.title: Wearable Sensors & Performance Analysis
WearableSensorsPage.subtitle: UWB and IMU-based human motion tracking and performance analysis
WearableSensorsPage.overviewText: Research into wearable sensor systems combining UWB (Ultra-Wideband) and IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) technologies for precise human motion tracking, fall detection, and sports performance analysis. This project spans controlled lab environments and real-world field experiments.
WearableSensorsPage.localizationText: A structured indoor test environment was established to validate UWB-based localization accuracy under controlled conditions. Multiple anchor nodes were positioned in a calibrated grid, enabling sub-decimeter positional accuracy measurements. IMU data was synchronized to provide complementary inertial measurements for motion state classification.
WearableSensorsPage.localizationImageAlt: Workstation display showing a precision localization and tracking interface used in controlled indoor tests
WearableSensorsPage.localizationCaption: Controlled localization test environment with UWB anchor placement
WearableSensorsPage.motionText: Collected sensor data was processed through machine learning pipelines to classify motion states, detect anomalies such as falls, and evaluate athletic performance metrics. The fusion of UWB positional data and IMU acceleration/gyroscope readings enables robust discrimination between normal activity and fall events with high sensitivity and specificity.
WearableSensorsPage.motionImageAlt: Abstract visualization representing large-scale motion and sensor-derived data for analysis pipelines
WearableSensorsPage.motionCaption: Motion evaluation pipeline — sensor fusion and ML classification results
WearableSensorsPage.fieldText: Real-world trials were conducted in sports and healthcare settings to validate system performance outside controlled laboratory conditions. Field experiments tested the system's robustness to multipath propagation, body occlusion, and varying environmental conditions, demonstrating reliable fall detection and performance analysis in practical deployments.
WearableSensorsPage.fieldImageAlt: Athlete on an indoor court wearing ankle-mounted sensors during a motion capture style field experiment
WearableSensorsPage.fieldCaption: Field experiment setup — real-world wearable sensor deployment

metadata.title: Warehouse Automation & Order Picking
metadata.description: Reinforcement learning and swarm optimization for multi-agent order picking in steel warehouses — research and simulation platform by D7 Technology.

WarehouseAutomationPage.title: Warehouse Automation & Order Picking
WarehouseAutomationPage.subtitle: Reinforcement learning and swarm optimization for multi-agent order picking
WarehouseAutomationPage.overviewText: Order picking is the single most time-consuming operation in warehouse logistics. This project treats it as a multi-agent sequential decision problem: given a warehouse layout, a product catalog and a set of customer orders, several picking vehicles must be routed to collect every item and return to the exit in the shortest total time, without colliding in shared aisles. The work targets steel warehouses, where products are long profiles stored across multiple slots and a single order may span dozens of locations.
WarehouseAutomationPage.approachText: Two families of algorithms are implemented against a common simulation environment so their results can be compared directly on the same layouts and order sets. The first is swarm-based: a time-dependent Ant Colony Optimization planner that builds a pheromone matrix over the warehouse grid and resolves collisions by treating occupancy as a function of time rather than space alone. The second is deep reinforcement learning — DQN, Dueling DQN, Double Dueling DQN and PPO agents, implemented in PyTorch, which learn a picking policy through repeated episodes instead of planning each route from scratch.
WarehouseAutomationPage.environmentText: Warehouses are described as JSON grid maps defining dimensions, aisles, loading zones, entrances, exits and item locations. The reference layout models a real steel warehouse: a 30 × 28 grid holding 289 distinct product types, each stored across several slots and linked to live order identifiers. A smaller 12 × 7 layout is used for rapid iteration during training. The environment exposes a standard step-and-reward interface, so agents and classical planners can be swapped without changing the warehouse model.
WarehouseAutomationPage.platformText: The research code is wrapped in a browser-based platform that makes experiments repeatable without touching Python. Operators upload a warehouse map, choose a planning algorithm, set training hyperparameters — episode count, learning rate, discount factor, epsilon schedule, batch size — and either train a fresh policy or run an existing one. Simulation runs are rendered back as video for inspection.
WarehouseAutomationPage.platformFigureAlt: Warehouse automation platform: map selection table and algorithm choice between ACO, RL and PPO
WarehouseAutomationPage.platformFigureCaption: Map selection and algorithm choice. Uploaded layouts are listed with their grid dimensions and product counts; ACO, RL and PPO can each be run against the same warehouse.
WarehouseAutomationPage.workflowText: The platform separates the people who define a warehouse from the people who order from it. On the operator side, warehouse maps and product catalogs are uploaded and managed directly or pulled from an existing endpoint. On the ordering side, a guided flow walks through selecting a warehouse, building an order from the catalog, choosing an algorithm and watching the resulting simulation.
WarehouseAutomationPage.workflowFigureAlt: Operator panel listing uploaded warehouse maps with dimensions, product counts and status
WarehouseAutomationPage.workflowFigureCaption: Operator panel. Warehouse layouts are uploaded as JSON and exposed to the ordering side, with product-type counts and last-updated timestamps.
WarehouseAutomationPage.catalogFigureAlt: Product catalog view showing steel profile product codes with per-item order quantities
WarehouseAutomationPage.catalogFigureCaption: Order construction against the 289-product steel catalog. Items carry their source order identifiers, and per-item quantities feed the picking problem handed to the planner.
WarehouseAutomationPage.statusText: The ACO planner runs against production-scale layouts, and the reinforcement learning agents train and execute on the same environment. Work continues on comparative benchmarking across layouts and order profiles, and on packaging the platform for a public demonstration deployment.
WarehouseAutomationPage.demoNote: A public demonstration of the simulation platform is being prepared.

metadata.title: Micro-Climate Forecasting: Rain & Wind
metadata.description: Live weather station data and rain and wind forecasts for the next 1, 6 and 24 hours — Single, Hybrid and Online models compared side by side, by D7 Technology.

MicroClimatePage.title: Micro-Climate Forecasting: Rain & Wind
MicroClimatePage.subtitle: Live readings and hour-by-hour wind and rain forecasts for our office window in Istanbul.

single.title: Single
single.text: Learns from this station's own readings. Best for the next hour.

hybrid.title: Hybrid
hybrid.text: Corrects the weather-service forecast with this station's readings. Best for 6–24 hours.

online.title: Online
online.text: Learns after every hour and blends all forecasts, trusting the most accurate one most.

MicroClimatePage.moreScoring: Every forecast is kept as issued and checked against the measurement once its hour has passed. Wind is scored by average error in m/s, rain chance by the Brier score (0 = perfect). The percentage shows how much better a model is than simply assuming “No change”.
MicroClimatePage.moreSystem: The station (ESP32 with wind, rain, temperature, humidity and pressure sensors) signs each reading, sends it every 5 minutes via a Raspberry Pi to our AWS server, which also downloads weather-service forecasts every hour and trains the models.
MicroClimatePage.moreModels: LightGBM models were pre-trained on 11 years from 13 nearby weather stations and are fine-tuned nightly on this station; SARIMA/SARIMAX start after 7 days of data. The Online blend also weighs the Weather.com daily forecast (12-hour day and night blocks spread over the hours).

dashboard.rawNote: Raw sensor readings. The station sits next to the building: temperature reads a few degrees warm and wind is sheltered.
dashboard.hourlyNote: Forecast: {method}. Wind and gust in m/s, arrows show where the wind blows.

status.nextHour: first forecast at the next full hour

dashboard.accuracyHint: Average error in {unit} (lower is better). % = better than “No change”.
dashboard.accuracyHintRain: Brier score (0 = perfect). % = better than “No change”.
dashboard.noScoresYet: Scores appear after the first forecasts have been checked.
dashboard.weightsHint: How much the blend trusts each model right now.
dashboard.testedTitle: How the models scored in testing
dashboard.testedHint: Before going live, both LightGBM models were tested on 6 months of data from nearby weather stations that they never saw in training. Bars show how much smaller their error was than “No change”.
dashboard.testedNote: Above 0 = better than assuming nothing changes. The raw weather service is far off at short range (bars cut at −60%) because it forecasts a grid cell, not the exact spot.
